coronodon.name: Coronodon havensteini
coronodon.heading: Cetacean Mystery!
coronodon.body:
A Crown of Teeth

Coronodon havensteini inhabited the seas off present-day South Carolina roughly 28–30 million years ago. Its original fossil was discovered in the Ashley Formation along the Wando River, near Charleston. Its species name honours its discoverer, Mark Havenstein.

Estimated at around five metres long, this early relative of living baleen whales carried pointed front teeth for grasping prey and broad, overlapping molars with multiple cusps. These crown-like teeth inspired its name: Coronodon, meaning “crown tooth.”

Could this hunter also filter seawater through its teeth? Researchers originally proposed that gaps between its molars acted as a sieve. Later research strengthened the evidence for active predation, while tooth-based filtering remains debated. Its unusual jaws illuminate the evolutionary history behind today’s baleen-equipped ocean giants.

zygophyseter.name: Zygophyseter varolai
zygophyseter.body:
In this reconstruction, Zygophyseter varolai is portrayed as a predatory sperm whale known as the “abyssal ripper,” characterized by deep mandibular alveoli—deep tooth sockets in the lower jaw. Measuring an estimated 6.5–7 metres, with some specimens suggesting over 9 metres, this formidable hunter carried 13 pairs of upper teeth and 14 pairs below. Its enamel-crowned teeth, substantial roots and powerful jaw-muscle attachments supported a formidable bite. Biomechanical simulations suggest it seized prey with its front teeth, then sheared it with stronger bites farther back.

Its almost complete skeleton was discovered by Angelo Varola at Cisterna Quarry near Cavallino, on the Salento Peninsula in Apulia, southern Italy. Preserved in the marine limestone of the Pietra leccese Formation, it comes from Tortonian deposits of the Late Miocene, dated in the original description to approximately 10.5–8.14 million years ago.

Zygophyseter belongs to an extinct branch of the sperm-whale superfamily, sharing evolutionary ancestry with today’s Physeter macrocephalus. A large basin atop its skull probably housed a spermaceti organ, connecting this ancient predator with the specialized acoustic anatomy of living sperm whales.
